summary: Teach children that a straight line is a half turn (180°) and a full point is a whole turn (360°), so the angles filling each are parts that share out a fixed whole. The load-bearing idea is additivity: an angle split into non-overlapping parts has a measure equal to the sum of the parts. Once the whole is seen as fixed, a missing part is found by subtraction without a protractor, and vertically opposite angles can be derived as equal rather than memorised. The conceptual jump is from 'measure each angle' to 'the whole is fixed, so the parts are constrained.'
misconceptions: Confuses the two totals — uses 360° for angles on a straight line or 180° for angles at a point.
Angle measure treated as non-additive / not conserved — insists on measuring every angle separately and does not believe a missing angle is determined by the others.
Does not recognise a straight line as an angle of 180° (a straight/half-turn angle 'doesn't look like an angle'), so cannot apply the rule.
Thinks vertically opposite angles are supplementary (add to 180°) rather than equal, confusing them with the adjacent straight-line pair.
Assumes the parts must be equal (splits 180° as 90° + 90° by default) regardless of the given angle.

activities.title: The shared-whole angle bench
steps: Watch a ray that pivots on a straight line, with two angle wedges filling it; each wedge shows its degrees and a banner reads the running total, e.g. '110° + 70° = 180°'.
Drag the pivoting ray and notice that one wedge swells while the other yields, but the total never moves off 180°.
Say aloud the moment you realise you no longer need to measure the second angle: it is whatever is left of 180°.
Switch to a point version where three or four wedges share 360°, and drag to see the total stay locked at 360°.
Open a crossing-lines view: drag the lines and watch the vertically opposite pair stay equal as everything turns.
activities.insight: The whole (180° on a line, 360° at a point) is fixed, so the parts are constrained; a missing part is whatever is left of the whole, and vertically opposite angles are equal because each pair shares the same partner angle to make 180°.

activities.title: Hide and predict the missing angle
steps: On a straight-line diagram with one angle given (e.g. 110°), state the other angle before any reveal and say why it must be that size.
Explain the reason in words: 'the two angles sit on a straight line, which is a half turn of 180°, so together they make 180° and 180 − 110 = 70.'
Repeat for a point where three or four angles share 360°, finding the missing one by subtracting the others from 360°.
Try a case where the ray is clearly not up the middle, so the two parts are visibly unequal yet still total 180°.
activities.insight: A missing angle is determined by the others through subtraction from the fixed whole; the parts need not be equal.

activities.title: Contrast the line and the point, anchor on right angles
steps: Sort a set of diagrams by which whole applies: 180° for angles on a straight line, 360° for angles at a point.
Tap a straight-line diagram to reveal '180° = half turn' and a point to reveal '360° = whole turn'.
Build the benchmarks: two right angles make a straight line (180°), four make a point (360°), and three make 270°.
Answer practice items that find a missing angle on a line and at a point, including an item that checks whether vertically opposite angles are equal (not that they add to 180°).
activities.insight: The two totals come from half-turn versus whole-turn; 270° is three right angles; vertically opposite angles are always equal, but they add to 180° only in the special case where the lines are perpendicular (both 90°), whereas adjacent angles on a straight line always add to 180°.

checkQuestion: Show a straight line with a point on it and one ray going up, making two angles. Mark one angle as 110° and leave the other blank. Ask: 'What is the other angle?' — and then, whatever they say: 'How do you know it has to be that, without measuring it?'
checkAnswer: 70°, because the two angles sit on a straight line, which is a half turn of 180°, so together they must make 180° and 180 − 110 = 70. (The reason — a straight line is 180° and the parts share it — is the part that matters.)
